# Progress note

This draft identifies the people who could benefit from coordinated load and resource management and describes a small research computing workflow. I used the National Science Foundation award abstract to understand why routing requests and allocating resources can interfere when they are handled separately. I also reviewed NGINX documentation to understand round-robin and least-connected routing as existing approaches. I narrowed my proposed contribution to a small application-level prototype with a fixed pool of workers and controlled test requests. The main open issue is whether queue length and recent completion times provide enough information to guide both routing and worker allocation. The stakeholder workflow is currently an assumption, and I have not collected interviews or performance measurements. My next step is to validate that workflow and define a repeatable workload for the prototype.

# 1 Problem research and scope

## Problem and affected people

I am investigating how a small service can coordinate incoming work with the workers available to process it. A load balancer decides where requests go. Resource management decides how much processing capacity is available to handle them. When these decisions use different or outdated information, requests may build up in one place while capacity elsewhere is underused.

My proposed target users are students and researchers in a university research group who submit data-processing jobs to shared computing resources, along with the developer or administrator who maintains that service. For example, they might submit files for a numerical summary and wait for the results before continuing their analysis. Delays affect their work, while the administrator must investigate queues and adjust worker assignments.

**Stakeholder assumption:** This university research group is a proposed use case, not a confirmed customer. I have not interviewed a specific lab or verified its infrastructure. Georgia Tech Research Corporation is the recipient of the source award, but I am not claiming that its staff requested this student prototype.

| Stakeholder | Task | Need |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Student or researcher | Submit a processing job and use its result | Predictable waiting time and a clear outcome |
| Service administrator | Manage a limited pool of workers | See where work accumulates and use available workers effectively |
| Application developer | Maintain routing and processing behavior | A simple way to coordinate decisions and compare results |

## Current workflow

**Assumed starting workflow:** A researcher submits a job to a service. A dispatcher sends the job to one of two processing services, each with its own queue and assigned worker processes. Workers process jobs and return results. The administrator monitors delays and adjusts assignments when needed. In the simple baseline, routing follows a fixed round-robin order and the worker allocation stays fixed.

The difficulty occurs when jobs take different amounts of time or the effective capacity of a service changes. Giving each service the same number of requests does not necessarily give each the same amount of work. Routing can continue sending jobs to a busy service even when another has capacity available. This baseline is an experimental starting point; it does not describe every existing load balancer.

## Concrete scenario

**Illustrative scenario, not a measured incident:** Two researchers submit a mixture of small and large files. Processing Service A is still handling several large files, while Service B has finished most of its smaller files. The round-robin dispatcher continues alternating requests between A and B. A new small job sent to A waits behind expensive work even though B could finish it sooner. The researcher waits longer, and the administrator sees an uneven backlog.

Normally, the submitted job should reach an available worker, finish, and return its result. The proposed investigation asks whether sharing queue and worker information can improve that sequence: the dispatcher could favor a service with available capacity, and a coordinator could move an idle worker to the busier service. If all workers are occupied, the service would need a clear limit on how much additional work it accepts. Whether these decisions actually improve performance remains to be tested.

## Evidence

The [National Science Foundation (NSF) Award 2542973 abstract](https://www.nsf.gov/awardsearch/showAward?AWD_ID=2542973), titled *CAREER: Integrated Load and Resource Management for High-Utilization Datacenters*, identifies the separation of resource allocation and load distribution as a source of inefficient resource use and slow responses to changing workloads. It also describes varying request demands, changing bottlenecks, and interference between control mechanisms. This supports investigating coordination, but does not establish that my proposed lab has this problem or that my prototype will solve it.

[NGINX's load-balancing documentation](https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/load_balancing.html) describes round-robin routing and least-connected routing. It explains that least-connected routing can help when requests take different amounts of time. This provides an existing approach to study and a reason to test more than equal request distribution. My prototype's benefit over an existing adaptive approach is an open question.

**Assumptions still to validate:** The target workflow has uneven job costs; workers can serve either processing service; queue length and recent completion time are useful indicators; and coordination costs will be small enough to justify the changes. 

## Six-week contribution

This semester I will investigate one small capability: using shared information about queued work and assigned workers to coordinate where a request is sent and how available workers are assigned. I plan to build a minimal coded prototype with two processing services, a small fixed worker pool, and repeatable short and long processing jobs. The initial working path will accept a job, route it, execute it, and return a result while recording its waiting and completion times.

Within that prototype, I will explore a simple admission limit and reassignment of idle workers between the two services. Running jobs will finish before their workers change assignments. I will compare the coordinated behavior with round-robin routing and fixed worker allocation under the same workload and total worker count. Initial evidence will include completed jobs, waiting or response times, and rejected jobs so that rejecting more work cannot be presented as a performance improvement. Detailed rules and test targets will be developed in later assignments.

## Semester II scope

The larger goal is a working, evaluated application-level manager that combines request admission, worker allocation, and routing across multiple service instances. Semester II will extend the initial path with more varied workloads, a comparison with an adaptive routing baseline, and tests of delayed status reports and changing capacity. A small chain of services can then be used to investigate backpressure: allowing a busy downstream service to signal upstream components to slow incoming work.

The NSF award's three thrusts concern request-level tracking and admission, integration with operating-system scheduling, and coordination across clusters and microservice chains. My project will explore simplified application-level counterparts: request measurements and limits, worker-process allocation, and routing/backpressure across service instances. It will not reproduce the award's operating-system or hardware research. The initial deployment can use separate communicating processes on one machine, with the shared-machine limitation stated in the results.

## Exclusions

* Kernel changes, hardware modifications, and microsecond-level control guarantees.  
* Automatic cloud purchasing, datacenter-scale deployment, and production use.  
* Moving or interrupting jobs that are already running.  
* Real institutional datasets, real user accounts, and deployment into a university's existing infrastructure.  
* Claims about reduced energy consumption or cost without appropriate measurements.  
* A full microservice chain, comprehensive recovery system, and polished user interface in the first six-week contribution.
